d: Full 45-minute mock interview of 'design a news feed', then switch seats and grade another candidate
goal: Your win today: run a full 'design a news feed' interview through all four steps on the clock, choosing strong moves at each step, then judge another candidate's run as the interviewer would.
bookSections: Whole chapter: the four steps, time allocation, the news feed example, dos and don'ts, red flags

stages.title: Step 1: Scope the Feed
stages.teaches: Applying step 1 under a clock: the same news feed facts as quest 3.2 (both platforms; publish + view friends' feed; reverse-chronological by assumption; up to 5,000 friends; 10M DAU; images and video), but now the learner must find them unprompted, with moves that cost time.
stages.interaction: Same layout as 0008: a sticky 45-minute clock bar with step label, a 'signal' meter, and an interviewer chat. Opening line from the interviewer: 'Design a news feed.' The learner gets a move menu each turn (4 options, mixed good/bad), e.g. 'Start drawing the architecture' (bad: interviewer interrupts, −signal, +2 min), 'Ask which features matter most' (good, reveals publish + view), 'Ask about scale now and in a year' (good, reveals 10M DAU), 'Ask about friend limits' (good, reveals 5,000), 'Ask whether posts have media' (good, reveals images + video), 'Ask mobile or web' (good), 'Ask about feed order' → interviewer says 'you decide' → follow-up menu where 'state reverse-chronological and write it down' is correct, 'assume silently' costs signal later, 'Ask about brand colours' (bad, −1 min, −signal), 'Ask about the existing stack' (good). Each good move costs 1 game-minute; each bad move 2–3 minutes. A requirements board fills as facts are revealed. Stage clears when all 6 facts are on the board; finishing within 10 minutes earns a bonus; past 10 minutes the interviewer nudges 'let's move on'.
stages.check: Q.quiz lock-in before moving on: 'Which assumption did you write down?' correct: reverse-chronological order (to keep v1 simple).

stages.title: Step 2: Sketch and Check In
stages.teaches: Applying step 2: the two flows, the box toolkit, and the check-in.
stages.interaction: Whiteboard SVG with two lanes (Publish, Read). Learner taps component tiles in whiteboard order; a component whose dependency isn't drawn yet costs a minute (e.g., Fanout service before Post service). Required: Publish lane = User → Load balancer → Web servers → Post service (+ post cache, post DB) → Fanout service → News feed cache, + Notification service; Read lane = User → Load balancer → Web servers → News feed service → News feed cache. Trap tiles (cost a heart, labelled as over-engineering by the interviewer): 'Blockchain post ledger', 'Custom consensus layer', 'ML ranking service (we agreed reverse-chron)'. Then a decision moment with 3 options: 'Keep going into details', 'Ask: does this shape work before I go deeper?' (correct, interviewer replies 'yes, and I'm curious about fan-out'), 'Declare the design complete'. Then an interviewer curveball: 'Where do the videos live?' → options: in the post DB as blobs / object storage + CDN (correct) / on the web servers' disks. The clock bar advances accordingly.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'The interviewer said they're curious about fan-out. What does that tell you about step 3?' correct: prioritise fan-out in the deep dive.

stages.title: Step 3: The Deep Dive
stages.teaches: Applying step 3: prioritise with the interviewer, avoid rabbit holes, ask for hints when stuck, think out loud.
stages.interaction: Three rounds, each a mini-scenario with 3–4 move options and time costs. Round A: pick a 15-minute plan from topic tiles (as in quest 3.4's planner) after the interviewer's hint: correct plans lead with fan-out, then feed retrieval; the EdgeRank tile is a trap that eats 8 minutes. Round B, 'Stuck moment': interviewer asks how to handle a user with 10M followers; options: 'Go silent and think' (−signal, +3 min), 'Think out loud: push is too costly here, maybe pull for celebrities; ask if they want me to explore a hybrid' (correct), 'Say it won't happen', 'Ask for a hint after sharing what you've tried' (also good, smaller signal). Round C, pushback: 'Why not just compute feeds on read for everyone?' options: 'Insist push is always better' (stubbornness flag), 'Agree instantly and redraw everything' (no reasoning), 'Compare: pull makes reads slow for users with many friends; I'd keep push for normal users and pull for celebrities' (correct). Signal meter and clock update after each round.
stages.check: Round results feed the scorecard; the stage clears when all three rounds are done.

stages.title: Switch Seats: Grade the Candidate
stages.teaches: Judging moves from the other side cements the dos, don'ts and red flags. A design can be technically fine and still get a no-hire if the process is poor.
stages.interaction: Mirror mode. A transcript of 'Candidate Riley' doing the same news feed prompt, ~14 lines covering all four steps with timestamps. The learner taps each line and tags it 'Strong signal', 'Red flag' or 'Neutral'. Lines include: 0:30 Riley starts drawing a load balancer immediately (red flag: no clarifying questions); 3:00 asks 'how many friends can a user have?' after being nudged (neutral/late); 9:00 draws publish and read flows clearly (strong); 12:00 never checks in, keeps going (red flag: no buy-in); 16:00 explains EdgeRank weights for 8 minutes (red flag: rabbit hole); 25:00 interviewer suggests pull for celebrities; Riley says push is always right and moves on (red flag: stubbornness); 30:00 proposes CDN for video with a clear reason (strong); 38:00 goes quiet for 3 minutes (red flag: thinking in silence); 41:00 'I think the design is complete, no real weaknesses' (red flag: never claim perfect); 43:00 asks 'is there anything you'd like me to go deeper on?' (strong). Then pick the overall decision: Strong hire / Hire / Lean no hire (correct: solid technical pieces, but skipped scoping, no buy-in, stubbornness and the 'perfect' close are serious process flags) / Strong no hire. Reveal shows which book rule each red flag broke.
stages.check: Pass if at least 10 of the lines are tagged correctly and the decision is 'Lean no hire'; otherwise show the correct tags and allow a retry.

stages.title: Step 4: Wrap It Up
stages.teaches: Applying step 4: bottlenecks, failure cases, operations, next scale curve, recap if useful; don't end before the interviewer does.
stages.interaction: Pick exactly 3 of 8 closing cards (same card set as quest 3.4's 'Land the Plane' but shuffled, with the wording varied), then 'Deliver my close'. The interviewer reacts per card. After delivery, a final beat: interviewer says 'Thanks, that's all from me. Any questions?' with options: 'Ask for feedback or ask about the team's real challenges' (good) vs 'No, bye' (neutral) vs 'So did I pass?' (weak). The clock bar should finish near 45:00; overruns cost signal.
stages.check: Stage clears on delivery; score feeds the final scorecard.

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior + Scorecard
stages.sub: The 60-second game plan, then your verdict
stages.teaches: A compressed, spoken run-through of the whole interview for the news feed, plus a scorecard that maps the run to the five signals from quest 3.1.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Give the 60-second version of how you ran this interview, step by step.' Model answer (our words): 'I started by scoping: mobile and web, posting and viewing friends' posts, newest first by assumption, up to 5,000 friends, 10 million daily users, images and video. Then I sketched two flows: publishing through the post service and a fanout service into a feed cache, and reading from the news feed service out of that cache, with media on a CDN, and checked the shape with the interviewer. In the deep dive I focused on fan-out, push for normal users and pull for celebrities, and on the retrieval path. I closed by naming the celebrity bottleneck, cache failure recovery, the metrics I'd watch, and what changes at ten times the scale.' After the drill, render a scorecard: five signal bars (Design skill, Collaboration, Under pressure, Ambiguity, Good questions) computed from choices across stages 1–5, total game-minutes used vs 45, red flags triggered (listed by name), and a verdict: Strong hire / Hire / Lean hire / Lean no hire. Store it under a separate localStorage key `sdq:v1:<lesson-id>-interview` (like 0008), wrapped in try/catch.
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I covered all four steps in order · I quoted the key scope numbers (5,000 friends, 10M DAU) · I named both flows and the fan-out trade-off · I closed with a bottleneck and an operations point.

caveats: The 45-minute game clock and per-move minute costs are our own game framing; the book gives ranges per step, not a scoring system.
Hire/no-hire verdicts here are a teaching device. Real decisions combine several interviews and company-specific rubrics; a single process slip rarely sinks a strong candidate on its own.
The fan-out details (hybrid push/pull, CDN for media) go beyond Chapter 3 and follow Chapter 11 and common practice.
Interviewers vary: some drive the deep dive themselves, some let you choose. The strong move is always to read their cues and check in.
